newsitem.title: POLAND: Foreign language deals cost Poland dear - auditor.
newsitem.headline: Foreign language deals cost Poland dear - auditor.

text.p: Warsaw's state auditor says Poland is losing huge sums because its negotiators sign contracts in foreign languages, newspapers reported on Saturday.
Rzeczpospolita daily quoted Supreme Auditing Chamber (NIK) President Janusz Wojciechowski as saying on Friday that such contracts should always at least be translated into Polish.
Among a long list of examples of losses he cited a 1992 deal with Italy's Fiat for privatisation of the FSM plant making small cars in Bielsko-Biala, southern Poland.
He said ministers had been given just a day to read a 1,000-page contract in English and Italian only.
"As a result the Polish side took on obligations that did not conform with our law, among other things concerning environmental protection," he told a news conference.
"The state treasury lost about 180 million zlotys ($64 million) on this contract," said Wojciechowski, whose chamber is the powerful watchdog over state administration.
Zycie, another daily, headlined its report of the comment by the NIK chief: "An expensive Italian lesson."

Andrzej Olechowski, the then finance minister who was one of the signatories of the Fiat deal and speaks fluent English, rejected the auditor's statement and said any losses incurred over FSM stemmed from earlier mistakes in building the plant.
So did Fiat Auto Poland chief Enrico Pavoni, who told Rzeczpospolita his company had taken over major debts of FSM and boosted its production.

"I have no idea where this figure comes from of 180 million zloty losses which the treasury was supposed to have incurred from the FSM privatisation," he said, adding that it was normal for such international contracts to be signed in a neutral language, especially in English.
But Wojciechowski said it was vital contracts be put into Polish as whichever language was used for them had a bearing on any later arbitration procedures should there be disagreement.
Polish experts are now drafting a law on the language which among other things will insist that all international agreements have at least a Polish version, on pain of fines.
